Carcassonne. The tile-placement board game designed by Klaus Teuber and released in 2000, named after a walled medieval town in southern France, where players draw and place square terrain tiles to build a shared landscape, claiming features with meeple tokens to earn points.

Each turn a player draws one tile and places it adjacent to the existing board, then optionally places a meeple on a road, city, monastery, or grassland to claim it. Meeples commit a player's pieces to incomplete features. Reclaiming them requires finishing the feature, creating a risk-reward tension that drives tactical play.

Completed roads, paths between intersections, award one point per tile. Completed cities award two points per tile plus two points for every pennant. Monasteries award nine points if surrounded by all eight adjacent tiles. The game's random tile draw and modular board ensure high replayability despite deterministic mechanics with no dice rolling.

The game won the Spiel des Jahres in 2001, cementing tile-placement as a major modern mechanic. Numerous expansions introduce inns, cathedrals, abbeys, markets, and variants like Carcassonne: Hunters and Gatherers or Carcassonne: The City.

Carcassonne is named after a real medieval fortified town in Occitanie, France, famous for its distinctive concentric walls and historical importance. It became a cornerstone example of elegant tile-placement design.
